scope: Primary-source evidence for dataset selection and scale, healthcare interoperability, HIPAA-aligned safeguards, and generative-AI risk management.

allowed_publishers: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
National Institute of Standards and Technology
evidence_policy.legal_caveat: This source register supports engineering decisions and is not legal advice. The architecture can support HIPAA-aligned safeguards, but software alone cannot be declared HIPAA compliant.

sources.title: Synthea
claims: Synthea generates synthetic, realistic but not real patient records.
Generated histories include medications, allergies, encounters, and social determinants of health.
The official project describes generated data as usable without legal or privacy restrictions and offers FHIR, C-CDA, and CSV formats.
caveats: Synthetic data is not evidence of clinical efficacy or universal population representativeness.
Embedded terminology terms are addressed separately in the repository NOTICE.

sources.title: Synthea Patient Generator repository
claims: The generator supports FHIR R4, Bulk FHIR NDJSON, C-CDA, and CSV exports.
The CLI supports a population-size parameter through -p populationSize and supports reproducibility-related seeds and a reference date.
The repository is licensed under Apache License 2.0.
caveats: Pin an immutable release or commit because the default branch changes.
CSV and Bulk FHIR exports require configuration.

sources.title: Synthea Downloads
claims: MITRE lists two SyntheticMass archives containing one million synthetic patient medical records in FHIR, C-CDA, and CSV.
The listed one-million-record archives are 21 GB and 28 GB and date from 2017.
The catalog describes the data as free from cost, privacy, and security restrictions.
caveats: The million-patient archives use pre-R4 FHIR versions and must not be used as evidence of FHIR R4 conformance.
One million patient records is not the same metric as one million relational CSV rows.

sources.title: Synthea Apache License 2.0
claims: The Synthea work is distributed under Apache License 2.0.
Redistribution conditions include providing the license, retaining applicable notices, marking modified files, and preserving NOTICE attributions when required.
caveats: The branch URL is mutable; preserve the license and notice from the exact pinned revision used.

sources.title: Synthea NOTICE
claims: The NOTICE identifies RxNorm material as public domain.
The NOTICE identifies LOINC content and its terms of use.
The NOTICE states that use of SNOMED CT is subject to IHTSDO affiliate-license provisions and describes territory/use qualifications.
caveats: Do not treat all embedded clinical terminology content as public domain.
Review terminology redistribution for the intended territory and use.

sources.title: Synthea CSV File Data Dictionary
claims: CSV export is configurable and produces normalized tables for patients, encounters, care plans, conditions, medications, observations, procedures, claims, and other entities.
The dictionary identifies primary and foreign-key fields needed for integrity tests.
caveats: The wiki is mutable; save the Synthea revision/configuration and generated schema manifest with benchmark evidence.

sources.title: MIMIC-IV version 3.1
claims: MIMIC-IV files are restricted to credentialed users.
Access requires specified training and execution of the PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data Use Agreement.
caveats: MIMIC-IV and sensitive derivatives are excluded from an unrestricted GitHub-ready repository.

sources.title: FHIR R4 RESTful API
claims: FHIR R4 defines read, version read, update, patch, delete, history, create, search, transaction, and capability interactions.
Servers choose supported resources and interactions and publish support in a CapabilityStatement.
The RESTful API does not itself define authentication, authorization, or audit collection.
caveats: Adapters must discover and test each EHR implementation instead of assuming every optional interaction exists.

sources.title: FHIR R4 Patient
claims: Patient represents demographic and administrative information about an individual receiving care.
Patient supports identifiers, active status, managing organization, and links to related Patient records.
An individual may have Patient resources maintained by multiple organizations.
caveats: A Patient resource id is not a universal person identifier; source-aware identity and merge policy are required.

sources.title: FHIR R4 CarePlan
claims: CarePlan describes intended care for a patient or group over time and can group activities, goals, and participants.
CarePlan status can distinguish proposed and active plans.
caveats: FHIR does not determine which of multiple active plans is authoritative or 'latest'; the deployment must define a deterministic selection rule.

sources.title: FHIR R4 Appointment
claims: Appointment represents a booking for a healthcare event at a specific date and time.
An Appointment may result in one or more Encounters; Appointment is administrative while Encounter has clinical implications.
caveats: Application documentation states require an explicit mapping rather than reuse of Appointment status.

sources.title: FHIR R4 Encounter
claims: Encounter represents an interaction between a patient and healthcare providers for care or assessment.
Encounter covers a lifecycle with statuses such as planned, in-progress, finished, and cancelled and includes status history.
caveats: The application's documentation states require an explicit mapping because they do not map one-to-one to Encounter status.

sources.title: FHIR R4 Composition
claims: Composition defines the structure and narrative content of a clinical document and supports clinical attestation context.
A Composition alone is not a document; it must be the first entry in a document Bundle with referenced resources included.
caveats: Target-EHR profiles, note type coding, authorization scopes, validation, and write behavior must be proven before claiming direct note submission.

sources.title: FHIR R4 Provenance
claims: Provenance records entities and processes involved in creating, revising, deleting, or signing a resource version.
Provenance supports authenticity, trust, reproducibility, and lifecycle assessment.
Provenance and AuditEvent overlap but serve distinct record-keeping and event-audit purposes.
caveats: Provenance does not replace security audit logging or an internal immutable note-version model.

sources.title: FHIR R4 AuditEvent
claims: AuditEvent records events for security logging, intrusion detection, and monitoring inappropriate use.
Relevant events include login/logout, access-control decisions, configuration changes, and data exposure to users.
AuditEvent update/delete is generally inappropriate because it would weaken audit-record integrity.
caveats: Audit records can expose sensitive data and need restricted access, integrity protection, retention policy, and monitoring.

sources.title: FHIR Bulk Data Access: Bulk Data Export
claims: The Bulk Data Access guide defines asynchronous APIs for an authorized client to request and retrieve large FHIR datasets.
The export API supports patient-, group-, and system-level exports with authorization limiting returned resources.
caveats: The guide does not provide a legal data-sharing framework, real-time exchange, data transformation, or patient matching.
Use Bulk Data only when the target server declares and proves support; protect generated files as high-value PHI.

sources.title: SMART App Launch 2.2: Launch and Authorization
claims: SMART App Launch connects third-party apps to EHR FHIR data using OAuth-based authorization.
SMART apps must support PKCE, and servers must support S256 rather than the plain challenge method.
Apps should request the minimum necessary scopes; public browser apps cannot protect a client secret.
Institutional authorization policy is configured in the authorization server and is not dictated by SMART.
caveats: SMART authorization does not replace application authorization, audit, privacy controls, or HIPAA risk management.

sources.title: Summary of the HIPAA Security Rule
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
claims: The Security Rule applies to covered entities and business associates and protects ePHI.
Regulated entities must implement reasonable and appropriate administrative, physical, and technical safeguards.
Risk analysis, risk management, audit review, periodic evaluation, and reevaluation are ongoing organizational obligations.
caveats: The page summarizes the currently effective rule and separately identifies proposed modifications; a proposal is not treated here as a current requirement.
A list of software features does not establish entity-level compliance.

sources.title: Guidance on Risk Analysis Requirements under the HIPAA Security Rule
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
claims: Risk analysis must cover the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all ePHI an organization creates, receives, maintains, or transmits.
Organizations must identify data locations, threats, vulnerabilities, current controls, likelihood, impact, and risk level and document the analysis.
The Security Rule does not prescribe one risk-analysis methodology.
caveats: Controls must be evaluated in the actual deployment and operational context, not only in source code.

sources.title: Guidance on HIPAA and Cloud Computing
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
claims: A service provider that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits ePHI on behalf of a covered entity or business associate is generally a business associate.
A provider maintaining encrypted ePHI remains a business associate even when it lacks the decryption key.
A HIPAA-compliant BAA and the parties' own risk analysis and safeguards are required when the provider is a business associate.
HHS OCR does not endorse, certify, or recommend specific technologies or products.
caveats: Encryption, zero retention, and no-training terms do not by themselves resolve business-associate or compliance obligations.

sources.title: Minimum Necessary Requirement
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
claims: The Privacy Rule generally requires reasonable steps to limit uses, disclosures, and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary for the intended purpose.
Policies should identify workforce classes, needed PHI categories, and conditions of access.
The guidance lists exceptions, including disclosures to or requests by providers for treatment.
caveats: Apply the standard with its regulatory exceptions and deployment-specific legal analysis; do not reduce it to a blanket technical rule.

sources.title: Are we required to certify our organization's Security Rule compliance?
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
claims: The Security Rule does not require an organization to certify compliance.
HHS does not endorse or recognize private Security Rule certifications as relieving regulated entities of legal obligations.
External certification does not prevent HHS from later finding a violation.
caveats: Describe the repository as supporting HIPAA-aligned controls rather than as HIPAA certified or inherently compliant.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2: Implementing the HIPAA Security Rule—A Cybersecurity Resource Guide
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
claims: SP 800-66 Rev. 2 provides practical resources for safeguarding ePHI and understanding Security Rule concepts.
NIST provides mappings from Security Rule standards and implementation specifications to Cybersecurity Framework outcomes and SP 800-53 controls.
caveats: The guide is an implementation resource and does not replace HHS regulations or entity-specific risk analysis.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
claims: AI RMF 1.0 is a voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific framework for managing AI risk across the lifecycle.
Its core functions are Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.
caveats: Using the framework is not a legal safe harbor or proof of clinical safety.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, NIST AI 600-1
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
claims: The profile defines confabulation as confidently stated erroneous or false generated content.
Its primary considerations include governance, content provenance, pre-deployment testing, and incident disclosure.

Suggested actions include documenting human-oversight roles, evaluating capability claims empirically, grounding retrieval data, monitoring post-deployment confabulation, and tracking errors and near misses.
NIST notes that laboratory, benchmark, or anecdotal testing may fail to reflect real deployment conditions.
caveats: The cross-sector profile must be tailored to the clinical documentation use case and does not guarantee elimination of hallucinations.
